message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may hold up to **one month’s rent** (or two if the lease is for a month‑to‑month tenancy).
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the landlord withholds part of the deposit. | | **Habitability** | • The landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control). | • Notify the landlord in writing (email or letter) of any needed repairs.
• If the landlord fails to act, you may file a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) or seek a court order. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are limited to **$25** per month (unless otherwise agreed). | • Keep receipts or bank records.
• If you’re late, communicate with the landlord and negotiate a payment plan. | | **Lease Termination** | • **Month‑to‑month**: Either party may terminate with **30 days’ written notice**.
• **Fixed‑term**: The lease ends automatically unless renewed or extended.
• **Early termination**: Some leases allow early exit with a fee; otherwise, you may be liable for rent until a new tenant is found. | • Provide written notice (email or letter) and keep a copy. | | **Right to Privacy** | • Landlords must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering your unit, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any entry notices. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR) or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major issue, you may **deduct the cost** from your rent (up to the amount of the repair) and pay the landlord the difference. | • Document the issue, send a written notice, keep receipts, and pay the landlord the remaining rent. | | **Eviction Process** | • The landlord must serve a **notice** (e.g., 3‑day notice for nonpayment, 30‑day notice for lease violation).
• If you do not comply, the landlord can file an eviction lawsuit. | • Respond to the notice promptly.
• Attend the court hearing and bring evidence of compliance or disputes. | | **Rent Control & Rent Increase** | • Texas has **no statewide rent control**. Landlords can raise rent at the end of a lease term or with proper notice (usually 30 days for month‑to‑month). | • Review your lease for any rent‑increase clauses. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify which utilities you are responsible for. | • Verify the lease and keep utility bills as proof of payment. | | **Insurance** | • Landlords may require renters’ insurance. | • Obtain coverage that meets the landlord’s requirements. | | **Legal Assistance** | • Free or low‑cost legal aid is available through local bar associations, community legal clinics, and the Texas Legal Services Center. | • Contact them if you face eviction, disputes, or need legal advice. | #### Quick Tips 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – It’s the primary document governing your rights and responsibilities. 2. **Keep Written Records** – Emails, texts, and written notices are your best evidence in disputes. 3. **Know the Timeline** – Notice periods and deadlines are strict; missing them can cost you. 4. **Seek Mediation First** – Many disputes can be resolved without court. 5. **Know Your Local Ordinances** – Some cities (e.g., Austin, Dallas) have additional tenant protections beyond state law. --- **Disclaimer:** This information is general and not legal advice. For specific situations, consult a licensed attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.
